$comment: The Project Path: one continuous build from an empty laptop to a running production platform. This is a learning graph laid over the existing labs — it never renames a lab or changes its id, it only says what order they make sense in and why each phase exists. A lab may appear here and in the library; a lab may also exist only in the library, which is correct for things like Terraform state recovery that nobody needs on their first pass.
title: Build the Production Platform
summary: One continuous project. Start on an empty laptop, finish with a containerised application running on Kubernetes on AWS, delivered by a pipeline that scans before it ships and watched by Prometheus — then break it on purpose.

productionProject.$comment: Where the path lands. The final phase ends with lab-19, which asks you to build the whole platform once with no instructions; this is the reference implementation of that same system, to read afterwards rather than copy from during. Kept in sync with the productionProject block in every roadmap — the same project, reached by a different route.
productionProject.title: Cloud DevOps Capstone
productionProject.summary: The platform you have been building, assembled and working: three microservices taken from source to a monitored, GitOps-managed deployment on AWS EKS. Terraform provisions the AWS infrastructure, Ansible configures the build host, Jenkins builds and scans, Argo CD reconciles, Prometheus watches.
productionProject.summaryAr: المنصة التي كنت تبنيها، مجمّعة وتعمل: ثلاث microservices من الكود المصدري حتى نشر يعمل ويخضع للمراقبة ويُدار عبر GitOps على AWS EKS.

guidedBuild.$comment: The same platform with the files removed. The hero promises "you build it, phase by phase" — this is that, and it belongs ahead of the reference implementation: derive it first, check yourself second.
guidedBuild.title: Build It Yourself — Cloud DevOps Capstone
guidedBuild.titleAr: ابنِه بنفسك — مشروع Cloud DevOps الختامي
guidedBuild.summary: Eight guided modules that build the same platform from an empty workspace. You write every line; the finished repository is the answer key, not the starting point.
guidedBuild.summaryAr: ثمانية modules موجّهة تبني نفس المنصة من مساحة عمل فارغة. أنت تكتب كل سطر، والمستودع المكتمل ورقة إجابة لا نقطة بداية.

phases.title: Foundations
phases.why: Everything after this assumes you can operate a Linux server, follow a network failure to its cause, and work safely in Git. Skipping these is what makes Kubernetes feel like magic later.
phases.milestone: You can administer a server, diagnose a connection, and recover work you thought you had destroyed.

phases.title: The application, in containers
phases.why: Before any cloud infrastructure exists, you need something worth deploying. Build and run the application locally so that AWS and Kubernetes are moving a real thing rather than an abstraction.
phases.milestone: The application runs locally in production-shaped containers, behind a reverse proxy, over TLS.

phases.title: AWS by hand
phases.why: Learn the cloud primitives in the console and CLI first. A VPC you have only ever seen through Terraform is one you cannot debug at 3am, when the console is what you have.
phases.milestone: You can build a network, grant least privilege, serve a site through a CDN, and restore a database — without any automation.

phases.title: Infrastructure as Code
phases.why: Now make it reproducible. Terraform's own concepts come first — provider, resource, state — and only then the real infrastructure, so each apply is something you can read rather than copy.
phases.milestone: The AWS environment is described in version-controlled modules with remote, locked state.

phases.title: Configuration management
phases.why: Terraform builds the machines; something has to configure them. Ansible is where a fresh server becomes a working one without anyone logging in — and where you learn why running it twice has to be safe.
phases.milestone: A new server is provisioned and configured with no manual steps, and a second run changes nothing.

phases.title: Kubernetes
phases.why: The application already runs in containers and the infrastructure already exists. Now there is an actual reason for an orchestrator — and the objects come before the cluster, so the cluster is not the first thing you meet.
phases.milestone: The application runs on Kubernetes with storage, routing, scoped permissions, network policy and autoscaling.

phases.title: Packaging
phases.why: A directory of manifests is not a release. Helm turns what you have built into something installable, upgradeable and rollback-able across environments.
phases.milestone: The application installs from a versioned chart, upgrades safely, and rolls back in seconds.

phases.title: Continuous delivery
phases.why: Everything so far has been run by hand at least once. Now automate it, with gates that block rather than report.
phases.milestone: A commit becomes a scanned, tagged image and a deployment, with no manual step.

phases.title: GitOps delivery
phases.why: The pipeline stops at a commit. Something has to turn that commit into a running change — and it must not be a person with cluster credentials, or the whole point of the previous phase is lost.
phases.milestone: A version deploys because Git changed, and a change you make by hand does not survive.

phases.title: Observability
phases.why: You now have something running that people depend on. Metrics tell you that something broke; logs tell you why. Being able to answer both is what separates a deployment from an operated system.
phases.milestone: Metrics, logs, dashboards and alerts exist — and the alerts are ones a human can act on.

phases.title: Operating it
phases.why: The part most curricula skip. Anyone can deploy a system on a good day — this phase is about the bad ones, where nobody tells you what broke.
phases.milestone: You have diagnosed failures you did not cause, recovered state you deleted, taken a node out of service without an outage, and built the whole platform once with no instructions.

$graphComment: What each lab leaves behind, and which earlier labs produced the things it consumes. An edge is a real dependency, not the previous lab in the list — so `unlocks` can be derived by reversing `requires`, and the path can be checked for ordering that contradicts it.
